name: README.md
label: Read me first
text:
# gridmind

Gridmind is an offline-first Sudoku app and an interactive course about how
constraint solvers and machine-learning systems reason.

**Play is the product foundation.** You can solve a Sudoku comfortably on a
phone or desktop, use pencil marks, undo mistakes, resume on the same device,
ask for explainable hints, and watch propagation and backtracking work.

**Learn is the primary curriculum.** Fifty lessons move from representation and
constraint propagation through supervised learning, learned search, computer
vision, model deployment, and browser inference. The reading and interactive
experiments are bundled into the static app; they require no shell, server,
Python environment, account, or network connection after installation.

Live app: https://sks-balan.github.io/gridmind/

## Start here

1. Open **Play** and complete a puzzle by hand.
2. Use **Hint** when stuck. Hints prefer deductions and explain dead ends before
   revealing anything.
3. Open **Learn** and follow the stages in order. Interactive labs run in the
   page, and completion progress stays only in the current browser.
4. Use **Docs** for the product and curriculum design, and **Code** to inspect
   the educational source that is safe to publish.

## Offline model

The production build is a static Progressive Web App:

- Sudoku solving, hints, lessons, labs, docs, and source browsing run locally.
- A generated service worker precaches every production asset, including the
  JSON lesson bundles, on the first successful load.
- The manifest supports installation to a desktop or phone home screen.
- No puzzle, progress, or custom input is uploaded. Game and lesson progress
  use browser-local storage only.
- Relative asset paths keep the build compatible with GitHub Pages subpaths.

The public `gridmind` repository contains only the generated site. The private
`gridmind-labs` repository contains source, curriculum tooling, tests, and the
optional developer labs.

## How the solver works

The exact solver first propagates naked and hidden singles over bitmask
domains. If inference stalls, depth-first search branches on the cell with the
fewest candidates (MRV) and orders values by least constraining value (LCV).
Every branch is verified; the solver never substitutes a model prediction for
correctness.

The TypeScript browser solver and Python reference solver have parity tests for
solutions and node counts. The hint engine separately tests deductions,
refutations, ambiguity, conflicts, and minimal backtracking.

## Learning design

The course has two intentionally separate tracks:

- **Browser course (primary):** complete explanations, checkpoints, progress,
  and interactive experiments that are meaningful in a static offline app.
- **Developer labs (optional):** source exercises for learners who want to
  implement algorithms, train models, and reproduce measurements locally.

The browser never displays a shell command as though it can execute it. See
[LEARNING.md](LEARNING.md) for the course contract and [CURRICULUM.md](CURRICULUM.md)
for all fifty lessons.

## Optional developer setup

This section is for contributors and source-lab learners, not users of the
static app.

The repository currently uses its established Python 3.13 `uv` environment and
Node/fnm toolchain. From a private checkout:

```bash
uv venv --python 3.13
uv pip sync requirements.lock.txt
uv pip install --no-deps -e .
cd web && npm ci
```

Checks:

```bash
.venv/bin/gridmind selfcheck
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests -q
cd web && npm test && npm run build
```

The build is self-contained in `web/dist/`. Publishing is a separate,
privacy-audited operation and is never part of ordinary development.

## Repository layout

```text
src/gridmind/       Python reference implementation
web/src/core/       TypeScript solver, hints, and session validation
web/src/ui/         game, learning, documentation, and interactive labs
lessons/            optional source-code labs and long-form theory
tools/              curriculum, bundle, puzzle, and privacy tooling
tests/              Python reference tests
scripts/            local server and explicit publish workflows
```

## Privacy and publishing

The source repository is private, but selected educational files are bundled
into the public Code view. Bundle generation uses an allowlist, and the publish
workflow audits the finished static output for credentials, email addresses,
and local absolute paths. Private session context, environment files, Git
metadata, deployment scripts, and generated training artifacts are excluded.

name: LEARNING.md
label: How learning works
text:
# How learning works

Gridmind teaches machine learning through a problem with exact ground truth.
A Sudoku solver can generate unlimited labelled examples and verify every
prediction, which makes ideas such as representation, leakage, calibration,
search guidance, and hybrid systems measurable rather than abstract.

## The browser course is the course

The **Learn** view is complete static content. A learner can read every lesson,
run the included interactive experiments, mark progress, and revisit results
with no local development environment. Nothing in this track asks the browser
to run Python or pretends that a shell command is an in-app action.

Each lesson has:

- a focused objective and vocabulary;
- a concise learning path and checkpoint;
- a complete deep dive with formal reasoning, pitfalls, and references;
- an interactive lab where direct manipulation materially improves the idea;
- local-only completion progress.

Interactive coverage begins with the concepts that most benefit from immediate
feedback: search cost, encodings, grouped data splits, whole-grid accuracy,
iterative decoding, and hybrid search. The lab registry is deliberately small
and extensible; new labs must teach an idea, not merely animate the page.

## The optional developer track

Some learning outcomes require real model training, controlled datasets, or
implementation work. Those are valuable but cannot honestly run inside a small
static page. The private source repository therefore contains a separate
developer track with Python and TypeScript exercises.

Developer labs may ask the learner to implement code, run benchmarks, train a
model, or record a result. They are optional extensions of the corresponding
browser lesson and are clearly identified as such.

## Offline boundaries

- The static app ships all lesson text and interactive code.
- The service worker precaches the production build after the first load.
- Puzzle and lesson progress stay in browser-local storage.
- No account, analytics service, model API, or remote notebook is required.
- Large model-training runs belong to the optional source track; exported,
  size-bounded models may later be bundled for offline browser inference.

## What success means

The course is successful when a learner can explain why a method works, predict
how a change affects a measurable result, and distinguish an exact solver from
a learned heuristic. Completing source code is useful evidence, but it is not
the definition of learning and it is not required to use the app.

name: DESIGN.md
label: Design notes
text:
# Product and learning design

Gridmind has one product with three layers. Each layer has a clear contract.

## 1. Play: correctness and trust

The Sudoku experience must stand on its own before it teaches anything else.
It supports touch and keyboard input, pencil marks, undo/redo, automatic
conflict feedback, resumable local state, explainable hints, custom puzzles,
and an exact solution path. Desktop and mobile share the same state model.

Hints are deliberately tiered:

1. report visible conflicts;
2. prove a naked or hidden single;
3. refute candidates when that proves one remaining value;
4. detect a dead branch and offer minimal backtracking;
5. reveal only when the puzzle has a unique solution and deduction is exhausted.

An ambiguous custom board is never told that one arbitrary completion is
forced. A model prediction is never presented as truth without solver
verification.

## 2. Observe: make reasoning visible

The exact solver emits events for givens, deductions, branches,
contradictions, backtracks, and completion. The interface can replay those
events without coupling rendering to the solver. Node count—not wall-clock
time—is the primary measure of search quality.

This layer bridges the game and the course. A learner first experiences a
useful feature, then opens Learn to understand the algorithm behind it.

## 3. Learn: browser first, developer optional

The primary course is a static offline browser experience. Lesson text,
checkpoints, progress, and interactive labs are bundled at build time. Local
commands and editable exercise stubs do not appear as browser actions.

The private repository keeps optional developer labs for outcomes that require
real implementation or training. This separation is honest about platform
limits without reducing the depth of the ML curriculum.

## Why Sudoku works for ML education

A solver is an exact oracle. It generates unlimited labelled pairs and verifies
every prediction, so learners can focus on the parts of ML that usually fail
silently:

- representation and inductive bias;
- train/validation leakage through augmentation;
- cell accuracy versus whole-grid accuracy;
- calibration and failure analysis;
- learned heuristics inside exact search;
- the boundary between perception, prediction, and verification.

The central measurements are whole-grid accuracy, grouped evaluation splits,
and search nodes. These principles recur throughout all fifty lessons.

## Static and offline architecture

Vite emits relative assets for GitHub Pages. A deterministic post-build step
enumerates the hashed output and writes a service worker that precaches the
entire app. Lessons, puzzles, docs, and the public source allowlist are JSON
bundles. Heavy editor and lesson code is loaded only when its view is opened.

Browser storage is optional and defensive: corrupt or unavailable state is
ignored, never allowed to block startup. No server receives puzzles or progress.

## Public/private boundary

`gridmind-labs` is private source. `gridmind` is generated public output. The
public Code view is an explicit allowlist rather than a repository dump.
Publishing audits the finished build for credentials, email addresses, and
local absolute paths. Deployment scripts, environment files, session context,
Git history, and training artifacts remain private.

## Quality gates

- Python reference tests and end-to-end self-check pass.
- TypeScript solver, hint, and session tests pass.
- Type checking and production build pass without bundle-size warnings.
- The generated service worker lists every production asset.
- Desktop and phone flows are exercised in a real browser.
- Tab, grid, focus, label, target-size, and reduced-motion behavior are checked.
- Publishing remains an explicit operation; normal development never mutates
  the public repository.

name: CURRICULUM.md
label: Curriculum
text:
# Curriculum

50 lessons in 9 stages: 25 ML, 11 Classical AI, 6 Engineering, 5 Frontend, 3 Computer Vision.

The **Learn** view is the primary curriculum: complete reading, local
progress, and browser-native experiments that work without a server or
Python environment. Work the stages in order; the measurement discipline
from Stage 0 is what makes every later claim meaningful.

The private source repository also contains optional developer labs for
implementing the algorithms. Those labs complement the browser course;
they are not prerequisites for using the static app.

## Stage 0 — Classical foundations

_How the problem is structured and solved by rules alone._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 01 | [Board representation and validation](lessons/01_board_representation/README.md) | Engineering | Settle how a puzzle is stored, parsed, printed and checked, because every later stage inherits this choice. |
| 02 | [Units, peers, and the constraint graph](lessons/02_units_and_peers/README.md) | Classical AI | Derive the structure of the puzzle once, and see sudoku for what it is: graph colouring on a 20-regular graph. |
| 03 | [Constraint propagation: naked and hidden singles](lessons/03_constraint_propagation/README.md) | Classical AI | Implement the two inference rules that solve most puzzles without any search at all. |
| 04 | [Arc consistency (AC-3), and its limits](lessons/04_arc_consistency/README.md) | Classical AI | Implement the textbook algorithm, then discover it buys you nothing over naked singles here -- and understand exactly why. |
| 05 | [Backtracking search and its heuristics](lessons/05_backtracking_search/README.md) | Classical AI | Add search on top of propagation, then watch good heuristics cut the search tree by orders of magnitude. |
| 06 | [Exact cover: Algorithm X and dancing links](lessons/06_exact_cover_dlx/README.md) | Classical AI | Re-cast sudoku as an exact cover problem and implement Knuth's DLX, a completely different and very fast attack. |
| 07 | [Puzzle generation and uniqueness](lessons/07_puzzle_generation/README.md) | Classical AI | Build the data source the whole repo runs on: well-formed puzzles with exactly one solution. |
| 08 | [Benchmarking and difficulty proxies](lessons/08_benchmark_harness/README.md) | Engineering | Build the measurement discipline every later claim depends on. Nothing after this is believable without it. |

## Stage 1 — Data

_Turning a solver into an unlimited, honest data source._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 09 | [Tensors, encoding, and the shape of the problem](lessons/09_tensors_and_encoding/README.md) | ML | Move from numpy arrays to torch tensors and decide how a grid becomes model input. |
| 10 | [Symmetry augmentation](lessons/10_symmetry_augmentation/README.md) | ML | Exploit sudoku's symmetry group for near-free data, and understand precisely what that data is worth. |
| 11 | [Splits, grouping, and leakage](lessons/11_splits_and_leakage/README.md) | ML | Make the leakage mistake on purpose, measure how big a lie it tells, then fix it permanently. |

## Stage 2 — Supervised deep learning

_Teaching a network to fill the grid, and finding out where it stops._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 12 | [A training loop, written by hand](lessons/12_training_loop_from_scratch/README.md) | ML | Build an MLP baseline and write the loop yourself: forward, loss, backward, step. No framework helpers. |
| 13 | [Autograd, optimizers, and schedules](lessons/13_autograd_optimizers_schedules/README.md) | ML | Understand what the loop is actually doing, and how the knobs change it. |
| 14 | [Convolutions, and why they are a poor fit here](lessons/14_convolutions_on_the_grid/README.md) | ML | Build a CNN, beat the MLP, then articulate why convolution's core assumption is wrong for sudoku. |
| 15 | [Architectures that know about units](lessons/15_constraint_aware_architectures/README.md) | ML | Build the inductive bias in directly: let the network attend along rows, columns and boxes. |
| 16 | [Transformers over 81 tokens](lessons/16_transformers_over_the_grid/README.md) | ML | Treat the grid as a short sequence and let attention learn the constraint structure itself. |
| 17 | [Iterative decoding: the confidence trick](lessons/17_iterative_decoding/README.md) | ML | The pivotal lesson. Stop asking for 81 answers at once; fill the most confident cell, re-run, repeat. |
| 18 | [Loss design and masking](lessons/18_loss_design_and_masking/README.md) | ML | Get the objective right: score only what the model should be predicting. |
| 19 | [Calibration and failure analysis](lessons/19_calibration_and_failure_analysis/README.md) | ML | Find out where and how the model fails, which matters more than its headline number. |

## Stage 3 — Learned search

_Keeping the symbolic solver, learning the decisions inside it._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 20 | [The solver as an environment](lessons/20_solver_as_environment/README.md) | Engineering | Instrument the classical solver so a learned policy can make its decisions. |
| 21 | [Imitation learning for variable ordering](lessons/21_imitation_learning_for_ordering/README.md) | ML | Train a model to copy MRV, confirm it matches, then try to beat the teacher. |
| 22 | [Graph neural networks on the constraint graph](lessons/22_graph_neural_networks/README.md) | ML | Use the actual structure from Lesson 02 as the computation graph. |
| 23 | [Reinforcement learning for heuristic selection](lessons/23_reinforcement_learning/README.md) | ML | Treat 'which heuristic to use at this node' as a decision problem with delayed reward. |
| 24 | [The hybrid solver](lessons/24_neural_guided_search/README.md) | ML | Put it together: symbolic search for correctness, learned policy for speed. Neither alone is enough. |

## Stage 4 — Perception

_Getting a puzzle out of a photograph._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 25 | [Finding the grid in a photograph](lessons/25_classical_cv_pipeline/README.md) | Computer Vision | Classical computer vision, no learning: locate the puzzle and flatten it. |
| 26 | [Cell extraction and empty detection](lessons/26_cell_extraction/README.md) | Computer Vision | Split the warped grid into 81 crops and decide which contain a digit at all. |
| 27 | [Digit classification with MNIST](lessons/27_digit_classification_mnist/README.md) | ML | Train the digit classifier. MNIST is cached locally in `data/raw`, so this works offline. |
| 28 | [The domain gap](lessons/28_the_domain_gap/README.md) | ML | Watch a 99%-accurate MNIST model fall apart on printed puzzle digits, and fix it. |
| 29 | [Synthetic training data](lessons/29_synthetic_image_generation/README.md) | Computer Vision | Render your own puzzle images from generated puzzles, with known labels, entirely offline. |
| 30 | [Photo to solution, end to end](lessons/30_end_to_end_photo_to_solution/README.md) | ML | Assemble the whole pipeline, then confront error propagation -- and use the solver to repair the model. |

## Stage 5 — Difficulty and generation

_Modelling how hard a puzzle is, then building to order._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 31 | [What makes a puzzle hard?](lessons/31_difficulty_proxies/README.md) | Classical AI | Interrogate the difficulty proxies, and find where they disagree with humans. |
| 32 | [Feature-based difficulty regression](lessons/32_feature_based_difficulty/README.md) | ML | Hand-craft features and fit a classical model. Establish the bar a network must clear. |
| 33 | [Learned difficulty from the raw grid](lessons/33_learned_difficulty/README.md) | ML | Predict difficulty from the grid itself and find out whether learned features beat hand-made ones. |
| 34 | [Generating to a target difficulty](lessons/34_conditional_generation/README.md) | ML | Close the loop: generate puzzles that hit a requested difficulty band. |

## Stage 6 — Beyond sudoku

_The same machinery on other constraint problems, including real ones._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 35 | [The same machinery on other puzzles](lessons/35_other_csps/README.md) | Classical AI | Prove the generality: point the solver at problems that are not sudoku. |
| 36 | [SAT encoding](lessons/36_sat_encoding/README.md) | Classical AI | Encode sudoku as boolean satisfiability and hand it to an industrial SAT solver. |
| 37 | [CP-SAT and global constraints](lessons/37_cp_sat_ortools/README.md) | Classical AI | Use a production constraint solver and see what a real `AllDifferent` propagator buys. |
| 38 | [Real constraint problems](lessons/38_scheduling_and_rostering/README.md) | Classical AI | The bridge out of puzzles: the same techniques on problems people pay to have solved. |

## Stage 7 — Deployment

_Shipping a model and being able to reproduce it._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 39 | [Model export and runtime parity](lessons/39_onnx_export/README.md) | Engineering | Get a trained model out of Python and confirm it still gives the same answers. |
| 40 | [Making the model small](lessons/40_quantization_and_distillation/README.md) | ML | Trade accuracy for size and speed deliberately, with the numbers in front of you. |
| 41 | [Running it in the browser](lessons/41_browser_inference_wasm/README.md) | ML | Ship the whole thing as a static page: WASM inference, no server, no upload. |
| 42 | [Reproducibility and experiment tracking](lessons/42_reproducibility_and_tracking/README.md) | Engineering | Make every result in this repo reproducible from a seed and a config. Retrospective, and the most valuable habit here. |

## Stage 8 — Browser and visualisation

_Building the interface: TypeScript, live visualisation, and models in the browser._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 43 | [Rendering the grid in TypeScript](lessons/43_rendering_the_grid/README.md) | Frontend | Build the 9x9 grid as real DOM with no framework, and learn why the browser is the right place to see a solver think. |
| 44 | [Interaction and state](lessons/44_interaction_and_state/README.md) | Frontend | Make the grid editable and give the user immediate, honest feedback about what they have typed. |
| 45 | [Porting the solver to TypeScript](lessons/45_porting_the_solver/README.md) | Frontend | Reimplement propagation and search in TypeScript, then prove the two implementations agree. |
| 46 | [Visualising constraint propagation](lessons/46_visualising_propagation/README.md) | Frontend | Draw the candidate sets and watch them shrink. This makes Lesson 03 visible rather than abstract. |
| 47 | [Visualising search and backtracking](lessons/47_visualising_search/README.md) | Frontend | Animate the search tree: guesses, propagation cascades, dead ends, and the walk back up. |
| 48 | [Running your model in the browser](lessons/48_model_in_the_browser/README.md) | ML | Load the ONNX model from Stage 7 and run inference client-side, with the classical solver as the correctness backstop. |
| 49 | [Visualising what the model thinks](lessons/49_visualising_the_model/README.md) | ML | Render confidence and attention over the grid. Interpretability is much easier to reason about when you can see it. |
| 50 | [Offline-first deployment](lessons/50_offline_first_deployment/README.md) | Engineering | Ship the whole thing as a static, installable site that works with no network at all. |
